Grocery Prices vs. Inflation in Canada: Milestone 3 notebook¶

CIND820 Milestone 3: Initial Results and Code, Samira Dadoun

This notebook runs the Milestone 3 pipeline from the clean data to the initial results, so it can be read without running the code (compiled copy: M3_initial_results.html). The same code is also kept as three scripts, run in this order:

Step Script What it does Output
5a model_data.py Builds the RQ3 modeling table: target, lagged drivers, month and event indicators data/clean/model_table.csv
5b models.py Seasonal naive baseline, linear regression, regression tree, random forest; assumption checks; comparison outputs/models/
5c results_rq1_rq2.py First results for RQ1 (categories by province) and RQ2 (grocer margins) outputs/results/

Steps 1 to 4 (get_data.py, clean_data.py, build_db.py, eda.py) were built in Milestone 2 and produce the clean files used here. All results use the frozen data snapshot of 2026-09-28. Run from the project folder: jupyter nbconvert --to html --execute M3_initial_results.ipynb.

1. Modeling table for RQ3 (model_data.py)¶

Block A, the target. y(t) is the monthly % change in the store-food CPI for Canada: (CPI(t) / CPI(t−1) − 1) × 100. The baseline, all three models and the metrics use this same quantity.

In [1]:
# Build the modeling table for RQ3 (CIND820 Milestone 3)
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd

CLEAN = Path("data/clean")

# ===== Block A: the target y(t) =====
cpi = pd.read_csv(CLEAN / "cpi_clean.csv")
food = cpi[(cpi["GEO"] == "Canada") & (cpi["Group"] == "Food purchased from stores")]
food = food[["REF_DATE", "VALUE"]].rename(columns={"REF_DATE": "month", "VALUE": "food_cpi"})
food = food.sort_values("month").set_index("month")
food["y"] = food["food_cpi"].pct_change() * 100
print(food.head(3))
print(food["y"].describe().round(2))

Block B, lagged drivers. Energy, agricultural commodity prices and USD/CAD are turned into year-over-year % changes; the policy rate stays a level. Each driver gets seven candidate lags (1–18 months). Only past values are used, so the model never sees information from the forecast month (no lag 0).

In [2]:
# ===== Block B: drivers as lagged features =====
drivers = pd.read_csv(CLEAN / "drivers_monthly.csv").set_index("month").sort_index()
table = food.join(drivers)

changes = table[["energy_index", "agri_index", "usdcad"]].pct_change(12) * 100
changes["policy_rate"] = table["policy_rate"]

LAGS = [1, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18]
for driver in ["agri_index", "energy_index", "usdcad", "policy_rate"]:
    for lag in LAGS:
        table[f"{driver}_lag{lag}"] = changes[driver].shift(lag)

print(table.shape)
print(table[["y", "agri_index_lag9", "energy_index_lag12"]].tail(3))

Block C, calendar and events. Eleven month indicators (one-hot encoding, January is the reference, drop_first=True) capture seasonality. Two event indicators use external dates, not the behaviour of y: COVID-19 (Mar–Jun 2020) and the invasion of Ukraine (Feb–Dec 2022). No scaling is applied: the linear regression is interpreted in original units and trees do not need scaled inputs.

In [3]:
# ===== Block C: calendar months and events =====
month_number = table.index.str[5:7].astype(int)
months = pd.get_dummies(month_number, prefix="m", drop_first=True, dtype=int)
months.index = table.index
table = table.join(months)

table["covid"] = ((table.index >= "2020-03") & (table.index <= "2020-06")).astype(int)
table["ukraine"] = ((table.index >= "2022-02") & (table.index <= "2022-12")).astype(int)

print(table[["m_2", "m_12", "covid", "ukraine"]].loc["2020-02":"2020-07"])
print("Covid months:", table["covid"].sum(), "| Ukraine months:", table["ukraine"].sum())

Block D, complete rows. The longest lag needs 30 months of history, so the first complete month is July 2019. Result: 86 months × 42 columns, no missing values.

In [4]:
# ===== Block D: keep complete rows, verify, save =====
lag_columns = [c for c in table.columns if "_lag" in c]
columns = ["y"] + lag_columns + list(months.columns) + ["covid", "ukraine"]
model_table = table[columns].dropna()

print("Model table:", model_table.shape)
print("From", model_table.index.min(), "to", model_table.index.max())
print("Missing values:", model_table.isna().sum().sum())

model_table.to_csv(CLEAN / "model_table.csv")
print("Saved: data/clean/model_table.csv")

2. Descriptive statistics of the target¶

Mean, median, mode, variance, a histogram and a boxplot by calendar month, plus an outlier check (1.5 × IQR rule). The mode is computed on values rounded to 0.1, because y is continuous.

In [5]:
# ===== Descriptive statistics of y (all monthly changes, Feb 2017 to Aug 2026) =====
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

y_all = food["y"].dropna()
summary = pd.Series({"count": y_all.count(), "mean": y_all.mean(), "median": y_all.median(),
                     "mode (rounded to 0.1)": y_all.round(1).mode()[0],
                     "variance": y_all.var(), "std": y_all.std(),
                     "min": y_all.min(), "max": y_all.max(), "skewness": y_all.skew()})
print(summary.round(3))

# Outliers: months outside 1.5 x the interquartile range
q1, q3 = y_all.quantile([0.25, 0.75])
iqr = q3 - q1
outliers = y_all[(y_all < q1 - 1.5 * iqr) | (y_all > q3 + 1.5 * iqr)]
print("Outliers (1.5 x IQR):", len(outliers))
print(outliers.round(2))

# Histogram (shape) and boxplot by calendar month (seasonality)
by_month = [y_all[y_all.index.str[5:7] == f"{m:02d}"] for m in range(1, 13)]

What this means for the models: the distribution is close to symmetric with no extreme outliers, so no transformation is needed. The boxplot shows a strong calendar pattern (January and November high, August and October low), which is why the baseline is seasonal naive and why the models include month indicators.

3. Baseline and models for RQ3 (models.py)¶

Split and baseline. The last 12 months (Sep 2025 – Aug 2026) are the test set, used once. The 74 earlier months are for training. The seasonal naive baseline predicts each month with the same month last year: y(t−12). Metrics: MAE (average error in points) and RMSE (penalizes large misses).

In [6]:
# RQ3 models: seasonal naive baseline + 3 models (CIND820 Milestone 3)
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error

CLEAN = Path("data/clean")
OUT = Path("outputs/models")
OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

data = pd.read_csv(CLEAN / "model_table.csv", index_col="month")

# ===== Split: last 12 months = test set, never used for training =====
TEST_MONTHS = 12
train = data.iloc[:-TEST_MONTHS]
test = data.iloc[-TEST_MONTHS:]
print("Train:", train.shape, train.index.min(), "to", train.index.max())
print("Test: ", test.shape, test.index.min(), "to", test.index.max())

# ===== Baseline: seasonal naive, prediction for month t = y(t-12) =====
naive_pred = data["y"].shift(12).iloc[-TEST_MONTHS:]

results = []
mae = mean_absolute_error(test["y"], naive_pred)
rmse = mean_squared_error(test["y"], naive_pred) ** 0.5
results.append({"model": "Seasonal naive", "MAE": round(mae, 3), "RMSE": round(rmse, 3)})

print(pd.DataFrame(results))
print(pd.DataFrame({"actual": test["y"], "naive": naive_pred}).round(2))

Linear regression. For each driver, the lag most correlated with y in the training months only is kept (all four chose 9 months). The regression uses 17 inputs: 4 lagged drivers, 11 months and 2 events.

In [7]:
# ===== Block 2: choose lags on training data, fit the linear regression =====
import statsmodels.api as sm

DRIVERS = ["agri_index", "energy_index", "usdcad", "policy_rate"]
chosen = []
for driver in DRIVERS:
    lag_cols = [c for c in data.columns if c.startswith(driver + "_lag")]
    corrs = train[lag_cols].corrwith(train["y"])
    best = corrs.abs().idxmax()
    chosen.append(best)
    print(driver, "->", best, "| r =", round(corrs[best], 2))

month_cols = [c for c in data.columns if c.startswith("m_")]
FEATURES = chosen + month_cols + ["covid", "ukraine"]

X_train = sm.add_constant(train[FEATURES])
X_test = sm.add_constant(test[FEATURES], has_constant="add")
linear = sm.OLS(train["y"], X_train).fit()
print(linear.summary())

linear_pred = linear.predict(X_test)
mae = mean_absolute_error(test["y"], linear_pred)
rmse = mean_squared_error(test["y"], linear_pred) ** 0.5
results.append({"model": "Linear regression", "MAE": round(mae, 3), "RMSE": round(rmse, 3)})
print(pd.DataFrame(results))

Assumption checks. Residuals vs fitted (linearity, constant variance), ACF (independence), Q-Q (normality), with Durbin-Watson, Breusch-Pagan and Shapiro-Wilk tests, and VIF for correlated drivers.

In [8]:
# ===== Block 3: check the regression assumptions =====
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats
from statsmodels.graphics.tsaplots import plot_acf
from statsmodels.stats.stattools import durbin_watson
from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import het_breuschpagan
from statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence import variance_inflation_factor

residuals = linear.resid
fitted = linear.fittedvalues

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4))
axes[0].scatter(fitted, residuals)
axes[0].axhline(0, color="grey", linestyle="--")
axes[0].set_title("Residuals vs fitted (linearity, constant variance)")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Fitted value")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Residual")
plot_acf(residuals, lags=12, ax=axes[1])
axes[1].set_title("Autocorrelation of residuals (independence)")
sm.qqplot(residuals, line="s", ax=axes[2])
axes[2].set_title("Q-Q plot (normality)")
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(OUT / "linear_assumption_checks.png", dpi=150)
plt.show()

print("Durbin-Watson (about 2 = no autocorrelation):", round(durbin_watson(residuals), 2))
print("Breusch-Pagan p-value (above 0.05 = constant variance OK):", round(het_breuschpagan(residuals, X_train)[1], 3))
print("Shapiro-Wilk p-value (above 0.05 = normal residuals OK):", round(stats.shapiro(residuals).pvalue, 3))

X_drivers = sm.add_constant(train[chosen])
for i, name in enumerate(X_drivers.columns):
    if name != "const":
        print("VIF", name, round(variance_inflation_factor(X_drivers.values, i), 2))

Regression tree and random forest. Settings are tuned with a 5-fold TimeSeriesSplit inside the training months (always training on earlier months), scored by MAE; random_state=42 makes the results reproducible.

In [9]:
# ===== Block 4: regression tree and random forest =====
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import TimeSeriesSplit, GridSearchCV

cv = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5)

tree_search = GridSearchCV(DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=42),
                           {"max_depth": [2, 3, 4], "min_samples_leaf": [3, 5, 8]},
                           cv=cv, scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error")
tree_search.fit(train[FEATURES], train["y"])
tree = tree_search.best_estimator_
print("Tree settings:", tree_search.best_params_)

tree_pred = tree.predict(test[FEATURES])
mae = mean_absolute_error(test["y"], tree_pred)
rmse = mean_squared_error(test["y"], tree_pred) ** 0.5
results.append({"model": "Regression tree", "MAE": round(mae, 3), "RMSE": round(rmse, 3)})

forest_search = GridSearchCV(RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, random_state=42),
                             {"max_depth": [3, 5, None], "min_samples_leaf": [2, 5]},
                             cv=cv, scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error")
forest_search.fit(train[FEATURES], train["y"])
forest = forest_search.best_estimator_
print("Forest settings:", forest_search.best_params_)

forest_pred = forest.predict(test[FEATURES])
mae = mean_absolute_error(test["y"], forest_pred)
rmse = mean_squared_error(test["y"], forest_pred) ** 0.5
results.append({"model": "Random forest", "MAE": round(mae, 3), "RMSE": round(rmse, 3)})

comparison = pd.DataFrame(results)
comparison["better_than_baseline_%"] = ((1 - comparison["MAE"] / comparison["MAE"][0]) * 100).round(1)
print(comparison)

4. First results for RQ1 and RQ2 (results_rq1_rq2.py)¶

RQ1: change in each food category minus the same place's all-items change, January 2019 to August 2026.

In [11]:
# RQ1 and RQ2 first results (CIND820 Milestone 3)
from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

CLEAN = Path("data/clean")
OUT = Path("outputs/results")
OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

# ===== RQ1: category gap vs all-items, every province =====
cpi = pd.read_csv(CLEAN / "cpi_clean.csv")
start = cpi[cpi["REF_DATE"] == "2019-01"].pivot(index="GEO", columns="Group", values="VALUE")
end = cpi[cpi["REF_DATE"] == "2026-08"].pivot(index="GEO", columns="Group", values="VALUE")
pct = end / start * 100 - 100

CATEGORIES = ["Meat", "Fish, seafood and other marine products", "Dairy products and eggs",
              "Bakery and cereal products (excluding baby food)", "Fruit, fruit preparations and nuts",
              "Vegetables and vegetable preparations", "Other food products and non-alcoholic beverages"]
gap = pct[CATEGORIES].sub(pct["All-items"], axis=0).round(1)
gap.columns = ["Meat", "Fish", "Dairy & eggs", "Bakery & cereal", "Fruit & nuts", "Vegetables", "Other food"]
gap = gap.sort_values("Meat", ascending=False)
print(gap)
print("Cells above +5 points:", (gap > 5).sum().sum(), "of", gap.size)
gap.to_csv(OUT / "rq1_gap_category_by_province.csv")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
image = ax.imshow(gap.values, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-25, vmax=25, aspect="auto")
ax.set_xticks(range(len(gap.columns)))
ax.set_xticklabels(gap.columns, rotation=30, ha="right")
ax.set_yticks(range(len(gap.index)))
ax.set_yticklabels(gap.index)
for i in range(gap.shape[0]):
    for j in range(gap.shape[1]):
        ax.text(j, i, gap.iloc[i, j], ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8)
fig.colorbar(image, label="Category inflation minus all-items inflation (points)")
ax.set_title("RQ1: food category gap vs overall inflation, Jan 2019 to Aug 2026")

RQ2: grocer gross margins (Loblaw, Metro, Empire) against the annual gap between food and all-items inflation. Descriptive only: margins are company-wide and fiscal years differ from calendar years.

In [12]:
# ===== RQ2: grocer margins vs the yearly food-price gap =====
margins = pd.read_csv("data/manual/grocer_margins.csv")
margins["gross_margin"] = margins["gross_profit_millions"] / margins["sales_millions"] * 100
margin_table = margins.pivot(index="fiscal_year", columns="company", values="gross_margin").round(1)

canada = cpi[cpi["GEO"] == "Canada"].pivot(index="REF_DATE", columns="Group", values="VALUE")
canada["year"] = canada.index.str[:4].astype(int)
yearly = canada.groupby("year")[["Food purchased from stores", "All-items"]].mean()
yearly_change = (yearly.pct_change() * 100).round(1)
yearly_change["food_gap"] = (yearly_change["Food purchased from stores"] - yearly_change["All-items"]).round(1)

rq2 = margin_table.join(yearly_change["food_gap"])
print(rq2)
rq2.to_csv(OUT / "rq2_margins_vs_food_gap.csv")

fig, ax1 = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))
ax1.bar(rq2.index, rq2["food_gap"], color="lightgrey", label="Food inflation minus all-items (points)")
ax1.axhline(0, color="grey", linewidth=0.8)
ax1.set_ylabel("Food gap (percentage points)")
ax2 = ax1.twinx()
for company in ["Loblaw", "Metro", "Empire"]:
    ax2.plot(rq2.index, rq2[company], marker="o", label=company)
ax2.set_ylabel("Gross margin (%)")
ax1.set_title("RQ2: grocer gross margins and the food-price gap, 2017-2025")
fig.subplots_adjust(bottom=0.2)
fig.legend(loc="lower center", ncol=4)
fig.savefig(OUT / "rq2_margins_vs_gap.png", dpi=150)
plt.show()

5. Summary and next steps¶

  • RQ3: all three models beat the seasonal naive baseline on MAE (0.518), none by the 10% target. The linear regression is the most balanced (MAE 0.488, best RMSE 0.550); the tree's lower MAE (0.472) comes from an almost constant forecast. Agricultural prices nine months earlier are the only significant driver; seasonality is the strongest effect.
  • RQ1: meat and other food rose faster than inflation in every province; fish rose more slowly in most; vegetables vary most by region.
  • RQ2: Loblaw and Empire margins rose gradually; weak correlation with the food-price gap (descriptive only).
  • Milestone 4: rolling-origin evaluation over several test windows, a combined cost driver, event-window sensitivity, category-level models, the Statistics Canada supermarket margin for RQ2, refactoring the scripts into reusable functions/classes, and a Power BI dashboard.
